reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Lichen sclerosus most often affects the anogenital skin, producing porcelain-white, atrophic, wrinkled or thickened plaques that are frequently intensely itchy or sore
It is commonest in postmenopausal women and prepubertal girls, but also occurs in men, where it can affect the glans and foreskin

In women the vulva may show loss of architecture with resorption of the labia minora, clitoral hood adhesions, and introital narrowing, often in a figure-of-eight distribution around the vulva and anus
In boys and men it can cause a tight, non-retractile foreskin (phimosis) and meatal narrowing
Extragenital lesions appear as white atrophic patches, classically on the trunk, and are usually asymptomatic
Long-term topical anti-inflammatory therapy and regular emollient use are the mainstays, aiming to control symptoms and reduce scarring and malignant risk
There is a recognised, though modest, increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma at affected genital sites, so persistent, thickened, ulcerated, or non-healing areas need biopsy
Arrange long-term follow-up to monitor for scarring, functional problems, and malignant change, and address sexual and urinary dysfunction sympathetically
reference.pathophysiology: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis thought to have an autoimmune basis, with associations to other autoimmune conditions and to specific autoantibodies in some patients. The characteristic histology shows epidermal atrophy, hyperkeratosis, a homogenised (hyalinised) upper dermis with loss of normal elastic fibres, and a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate beneath this zone. Genetic predisposition, hormonal influences, local trauma or the Koebner phenomenon, and possibly infective triggers have all been implicated. Chronic inflammation and scarring drive the architectural distortion, and sustained epithelial disturbance underlies the small risk of malignant transformation.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic eczema or lichen simplex chronicus of the genitals
Vulval or penile intraepithelial neoplasia and squamous cell carcinoma
Mucous membrane pemphigoid causing genital scarring
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy to confirm diagnosis in atypical cases and to exclude malignancy in suspicious areas
Screening or a low threshold for testing for associated autoimmune disease, such as thyroid dysfunction
Assessment of urinary and sexual function where scarring is significant
Photographic documentation to track architectural change over time
Referral for surgical assessment where phimosis or introital stenosis impairs function
redFlags: Persistent thickened, warty, ulcerated, or non-healing areas suggesting squamous cell carcinoma and requiring biopsy
Progressive scarring causing urinary obstruction or inability to retract the foreskin
Significant introital stenosis interfering with micturition or intercourse
New fixed nodule or enlarging lesion at a chronically affected site
Symptoms unresponsive to adequate treatment, prompting reassessment of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Lichen sclerosus is typically a chronic relapsing condition; symptoms and inflammation can be well controlled with maintenance therapy, but architectural scarring is often permanent and lifelong surveillance is advised because of the small risk of genital squamous cell carcinoma.
pitfalls: Dismissing genital symptoms as thrush or non-specific irritation and delaying diagnosis
Under-treating with only intermittent or weak topical therapy, allowing progressive scarring
Failing to biopsy persistent or changing lesions and missing early malignancy
Overlooking the condition in men and children, in whom presentation differs
Neglecting the psychological and sexual impact of chronic genital disease
management: Use superpotent topical corticosteroids (such as clobetasol propionate) for induction and maintenance to control inflammation and reduce scarring
Apply regular emollients and soap substitutes and avoid irritants to protect the skin barrier
Consider topical calcineurin inhibitors as a second-line, steroid-sparing option
Maintain lifelong surveillance with biopsy of thickened, ulcerated or non-resolving areas given the small risk of genital squamous cell carcinoma
Refer for circumcision in corticosteroid-resistant phimosis and for surgical release of introital stenosis or adhesions where function is impaired
Screen for associated autoimmune disease such as thyroid dysfunction
Refer to dermatology, gynaecology or urology, with attention to sexual and urinary function
